assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and Ye's demonstration of 10^-18 systematic uncertainty, turn atomic structure knowledge into the most precise measurements ever made. The magic-wavelength idea is simple and original, and the result gives a new tool for tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and a future redefinition of the second. It is a precision-atomic-physics result of the kind I trust: quantitative, with hard numbers, and ready to be built upon.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept in 2001-2003 and demonstrated the first strontium lattice clocks. Ye's group brought the strontium clock to the 10^-18 level and made the clock a many-body probe. Two laureates give a clean configuration. Others, such as Hollberg, Lemonde and Ludlow, contributed, and I am not sure how to weigh them (unverified from memory).
assessment.maturity: Independent groups (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE, NIST) have confirmed and compared lattice clocks for years, with agreement at the 10^-18 level. The field is mature and recognition is timely, since the 2012 prize covered ion trapping and cavity QED and left out clocks.
uncertainties: Possible competing credit to ion-clock groups (Wineland, Rosenband) and to the redefinition effort.
Whether the committee sees this as a precision-measurement tool or as a discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realise Hubbard-type models with tunable parameters. The superfluid to Mott insulator transition, fermionic Hubbard physics and single-site quantum gas microscopy let one see how quantum many-body states are built, which is the question I care about. The Jaksch-Zoller proposal and the experiments together make a coherent, lasting contribution to quantum many-body physics.
assessment.attribution: Zoller supplied the theory proposal (with Jaksch, Cirac and others). Greiner and Bloch performed the Mott insulator experiment in 2002 and developed the quantum gas microscope. Esslinger's group made central contributions on fermions, and Cirac has a separate claim in the theory. A fair split is hard because five names are credited, so I choose theory plus two key experimentalists. This is an uncertain allocation.
assessment.maturity: Many independent laboratories have reproduced and extended the results, so they are very well confirmed. The field is mature. The open question is whether quantum simulation has produced results beyond analogue demonstrations that a committee could single out.
uncertainties: Whether the 2002 Mott insulator work should be separated from the later microscopy and Fermi-Hubbard work.
Overlap with B011 (Cirac and Zoller) and B052, which could split recognition.
Whether Esslinger or Cirac should replace one of my choices.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The three-step recollision picture explains the high-harmonic plateau in a simple image: ionise, accelerate in the field, recollide. It is the conceptual basis for attosecond science and for imaging of electron dynamics. I know this field well, and I am aware of my own closeness to it, which I treat as a conflict to keep in mind and not as a reason to boost it. It is an unexpected and elegant idea with wide lasting impact.
assessment.attribution: Corkum's 1993 semiclassical model and the 1994 quantum treatment by Lewenstein and colleagues (with L'Huillier and Balcou) are decisive. Schafer, Kulander and co-authors proposed the same picture independently in 1993. Credit is shared and some key figures (Kulander, L'Huillier, Krausz) are already honoured or not on this list. I propose Corkum and Lewenstein but the allocation is contested.
assessment.maturity: Verified by many experiments, including HHG spectroscopy and laser-induced electron diffraction. The 2023 prize recognised the experimental attosecond pulses, and so a second prize on the theory may seem redundant to some committee colleagues.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2023 prize may reduce the case.
Independent simultaneous claims from Schafer/Kulander and from Corkum.
My own close connection to this community.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Trapping of antiprotons, antihydrogen and positrons, with precision comparison of CPT-tested quantities (the antiproton magnetic moment, antihydrogen 1S-2S spectroscopy, gravity tests), addresses a basic question about nature: why does matter dominate over antimatter? The experimental control is remarkable and the physics is fundamental, not technology driven.
assessment.attribution: Gabrielse led the single-particle trap measurements and trapped antihydrogen work with ATRAP. Hangst led ALPHA and the first trapping and spectroscopy of antihydrogen. Other leaders (Wolf, Doser, Yamazaki, Ulmer) have not been credited here. Two names is a reasonable configuration but the boundary of credit is unclear.
assessment.maturity: ALPHA, ATRAP and ASACUSA have confirmed the main techniques. Measurements are still improving and no violation has been seen, but the precision is already convincing. Timing is reasonable.
uncertainties: No CPT violation found, so the claim rests on technique and precision.
Credit among ATRAP, ALPHA, ASACUSA and BASE is not settled.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Aharonov-Bohm effect and the Berry phase show that phases in quantum mechanics carry physical meaning, and that gauge potentials and geometry have observable effects. This is a deep, original and clear insight, and it underlies later topological physics, from the quantum Hall effect to topological insulators. It speaks directly to what quantum mechanics is.
assessment.attribution: Aharonov and Bohm (1959) and Berry (1984) are the decisive contributors. Bohm is deceased, so he cannot share. Simon, Pancharatnam and others contributed to the geometric phase, which is a fair concern. Aharonov and Berry are a defensible pair, though it may seem odd to leave out Bohm.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by many experiments (Chambers, Tonomura, optical and NMR Berry phase measurements) and fully absorbed into textbooks. Recognition is very late, not premature. The risk is that the Nobel committee wants a more recent discovery.
uncertainties: Bohm's death and Pancharatnam's earlier work complicate the attribution.
Whether a theoretical concept without one decisive experiment fits the statutes.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED brings strong light-matter coupling, which I know from atomic cavity QED, into superconducting circuits. It is the platform of present superconducting quantum computers and gives clear quantum-optics experiments with artificial atoms. The idea is elegant and the results are solid.
assessment.attribution: The 2004 proposal by Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin and Schoelkopf, and the Yale experiment, form the core. Wallraff, who was first author on the experiment, does not appear on this credited list, which weakens a three-person selection from these names. I choose the three credited names with the strongest roles, but this is an incomplete credit picture.
assessment.maturity: Well reproduced worldwide and technologically developed. The 2025 prize recognised macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, which makes a further superconducting-circuit award less likely soon.
uncertainties: Wallraff and Nakamura are not in the credited list.
Recent 2025 prize in the same area may make recognition premature or redundant.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: BB84 showed that quantum mechanics can give communication whose security rests on physical law. It is original and simple, and it links the foundations of quantum theory (no-cloning, measurement disturbance) to practical protocols. It has had lasting influence on quantum information.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard proposed BB84 in 1984. Ekert's 1991 entanglement-based protocol is a separate, independent contribution and the list repeats his name in two spellings, which I treat as the same person. I keep Bennett and Brassard as the decisive pair but note that Ekert's claim is real.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally demonstrated over fibre and satellite links, with commercial systems. Security proofs are mature, though real implementations face side-channel issues. The 2022 prize on entanglement experiments partly covers neighbouring ground.
uncertainties: Ekert's contribution may require a third seat.
Whether the committee regards the work as physics or as computer science and cryptography.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Matter-wave interferometry with atoms gives very sensitive measurements of gravity, rotation and fundamental constants, and tests of the equivalence principle. It builds on laser cooling and Raman or Bragg beam splitters. The quantum-mechanical point (atoms interfering as waves) is clear and the precision is high.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard's early atom interferometer with gratings and Kasevich and Chu's light-pulse interferometer are decisive. Chu already has a 1997 prize, and Bordé's role, credited here, is on the theory of the Ramsey-Bordé interferometer. I propose Kasevich and Pritchard, though Bordé has a good claim.
assessment.maturity: Many groups have confirmed the technique, and precision gravimeters and gradiometers exist. Applications such as gravitational-wave detection and dark-matter searches are still developing, so some of the impact is still ahead.
uncertainties: Relation to the 1997 laser cooling prize and to the 2001 BEC prize.
Whether the fundamental-physics reach has been demonstrated or is still a promise.
